title: Who Checks the Algorithm?
objective: After this level you can explain how audits, explanations and appeal rights let people test and challenge automated decisions.
summary: Auditors test systems from outside, as the 2018 Gender Shades audit did; the GDPR can give rights to a human, to contest and to information, and New York City requires hiring-tool bias audits.

cards.headline: How do you test a system whose code you can't see?
cards.body: Most algorithms that choose for you are private. Yet researchers have found ways to check them from the outside, and some laws now give people rights when a machine alone makes a significant decision about them.

cards.headline: Testing from outside
cards.body: An audit asks whether a system behaves the way it should. If the code is public, auditors can read it. If not, they test from outside: send it repeated queries and watch what comes back, or run programmed fake users, called sock puppets, and compare how the system treats them. You learn what a box does by choosing its inputs and watching its outputs.

cards.fact: In 2018, Gender Shades found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women and at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.
cards.context: Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested three commercial gender classification products on a benchmark of 1,270 faces, balanced by gender and skin type. They sent in faces and compared the answers across groups. The gaps showed up only because someone chose the inputs carefully.

cards.headline: A right to a human
cards.body: In the EU, the GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing when it has legal or similarly significant effects on them. Where such decisions are allowed because they are needed for a contract or the person agreed, people keep at least the right to human intervention, to give their point of view and to contest the decision. They can also ask for meaningful information about the logic involved.

cards.headline: Audits by law
cards.body: New York City went further for hiring. Its Local Law 144 of 2021 bars employers from using an automated hiring tool unless it has had a bias audit within one year before use, a summary of the results is public and candidates are told. Enforcement began on July 5, 2023.

cards.headline: Checks: in place
learned: Auditors test hidden systems by choosing inputs
Gender Shades found error gaps across groups in 2018
The GDPR can give rights to a human and to contest
New York City requires bias audits of hiring tools

questions.prompt: Under the GDPR, if you agreed to a significant decision being made solely by automated processing, what can you still ask for?

options.label: A refund of any fees you paid
A full copy of the company's source code and training data
options.rationale: The right is to meaningful information about the logic, not the code.

options.label: Human intervention and a chance to contest the decision
A guarantee the decision will be reversed
options.rationale: You can contest it, but reversal isn't guaranteed.

questions.explanation: Where such a decision rests on a contract or your explicit consent, Article 22 guarantees at least the right to obtain human intervention, to express your point of view and to contest the decision.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones in checking algorithms in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Gender Shades came out in 2018, New York City passed Local Law 144 in 2021, and enforcement began on July 5, 2023.

questions.prompt: Like an auditor, you test a sealed box: it outputs 1 only when both of its inputs are 1. The logic gate inside is _____.

options.label: NOT
options.rationale: NOT has one input and flips it.

options.label: OR
options.rationale: OR would output 1 if either input were 1.

options.label: a half adder
options.rationale: A half adder has two outputs, a sum and a carry.

questions.explanation: An AND gate outputs 1 only if every input is 1. Choosing inputs and watching outputs is exactly how an outside audit works.
